chunks.content: 96 Why That 0% Interest Offer Could Backfire—Big Time Hi Sara, Let’s talk about something that gets ignored way too often in deal negotiations: interest rates on seller financing. Yes, I know. Not exactly a crowd-pleaser at cocktail hour. But if you’re buying or selling a business and you throw out a 0% interest promissory note thinking it’s no big deal… you might want to sit down. Here’s the deal: The IRS has this little thing called the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR). It's their way of saying, “If you lend someone money, we expect you to earn a certain minimum interest—or we’ll tax you like you did.” So what happens if the AFR is 4% and your deal includes a 2% interest rate on a $100,000 note? The seller only pockets $2,000 in actual interest—but Uncle Sam taxes them like they made $4,000. That phantom $2,000? Still taxed. That’s called imputed interest income, and it’s about as fun as it sounds. Now imagine that same problem with a 0% loan on, say, a $500,000 balance. The tax hit alone can be thousands of dollars… for income the seller never actually received. Why This Matters: When buyers pitch 0% interest seller notes, they’re not just asking for a sweet deal—they’re handing the seller a tax bill on top of the loan risk and inflation erosion. It’s like borrowing their car, returning it with no gas, and handing them a parking ticket for good measure. You can do better. Savvy buyers will either: Offer interest at the current AFR (Google it—rates are public), Or at least understand the risk they’re asking the seller to shoulder and explain why the structure makes sense. And if this is the first time you’re hearing about AFR or imputed interest? Please don’t toss a 0% loan in your LOI like it’s a hot tip from a Reddit thread. Bottom line: If you want seller financing to actually work, make it fair. Or at the very least, don’t make it tax-punitive. Ready to structure smarter offers that actually get accepted?
